places.name: Jaffa Old City & Port
places.ai_summary: Ancient Jaffa’s alleys, galleries, and stone wharves overlook the Mediterranean, blending Crusader remnants, mosques, churches, and lively markets. Wander artists’ studios, climb to the hilltop garden, and watch fishermen and yachts. Sunset light gilds domes and seafront restaurants, while history and myth mingle beside waves, breezes, and bell towers.

opening_hours.notes: Shops, galleries, and restaurants keep varied hours; weekends are lively.

places.place_tip: Arrive before sunset, explore alleys, climb gardens, then dine harborside. Bring camera, water, modest attire for sites, and patience exploring.
places.address: Jaffa Old City and Port, Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel

places.name: Tel Aviv Beaches & Tayelet Promenade
places.ai_summary: A continuous beachfront walkway links broad sandy beaches with cafés, playgrounds, and workout stations. Swim, surf, or cycle beside waves while lifeguards monitor seasonal sections. Sunset volleyball, musicians, and promenade skaters animate evenings. Accessible, family-friendly stretches offer changing facilities, rental chairs, and shaded spots along the lively Mediterranean urban shoreline daily.

opening_hours.notes: Lifeguard hours seasonal; check flags and posted conditions before swimming.

places.place_tip: Walk or cycle the promenade, hydrate, apply sunscreen, and swim only in guarded sections. Evenings bring music, volleyball, and breezes.

places.name: Rothschild Boulevard & White City Bauhaus (UNESCO)
places.ai_summary: Leafy Rothschild Boulevard anchors Tel Aviv’s White City, a UNESCO-listed ensemble of International Style buildings. Bike lanes, kiosks, and coffee culture meet striking architecture and Independence Hall. Stroll shaded medians, admire clean lines and balconies, and explore side streets revealing carefully restored modernist facades shaping Tel Aviv’s distinctive urban identity beautifully today.

opening_hours.notes: Buildings are private; join guided tours for interior access and context.

places.place_tip: Follow median path, read plaques, pause for coffee. Consider a White City tour for deeper insight into Tel Aviv’s modernist heritage.

places.name: Neve Tzedek Quarter
places.ai_summary: Tel Aviv’s first Jewish neighborhood charms with restored houses, boutiques, cafés, and galleries near the sea. Narrow lanes and wrought-iron balconies frame courtyards and murals. Suzanne Dellal arts complex hosts dance and performances. Explore slowly, browsing design shops and patisseries, then wander toward the beach for evening light along picturesque streets.

opening_hours.notes: Boutiques keep varied hours; evenings and weekends are lively.

places.place_tip: Wander side streets, peek into courtyards, and visit Suzanne Dellal. Finish at the beach promenade for sea breeze and colors.

places.name: Carmel Market (Shuk HaCarmel)
places.ai_summary: Bustling open-air market overflowing with produce, spices, street food, and clothing stalls. Vendors call out daily deals while aromas of falafel, bourekas, and fresh juices tempt. Expect crowds, color, and lively banter. Great for quick lunches, souvenirs, and people-watching along narrow aisles connecting Allenby and the beachfront neighborhoods nearby conveniently.

opening_hours.notes: Arrive early on Fridays; it becomes very crowded before Shabbat.

places.place_tip: Bring small cash, sample generously, and bargain politely. Protect valuables, and try fresh juices, halva, and warm pastries from bakers.

places.name: Tel Aviv Museum of Art
places.ai_summary: Israel’s leading art museum exhibits international masterpieces, Israeli modernism, and cutting-edge contemporary shows across striking pavilions. Architectural highlights include the Herta and Paul Amir Building’s twisting geometry. Expect world-class programming, sculpture gardens, and family activities. Rotating exhibitions reward repeat visits with fresh perspectives on global and local artistic dialogues and creativity.

opening_hours.notes: Hours vary on holidays; check website for exhibitions and tickets.

places.place_tip: Book tickets online for special shows. Start with the Amir Building, then the sculpture garden. Take breaks at the café thoughtfully.
places.address: 27 Shaul Hamelech Blvd, Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel

places.name: ANU – Museum of the Jewish People
places.ai_summary: Expansive multimedia museum at Tel Aviv University exploring Jewish identity, culture, migrations, and creativity across millennia. Immersive galleries combine artifacts, art, and personal stories. Family-friendly interactives engage all ages. Rotating programs, genealogy resources, and major temporary exhibitions deepen understanding of global Jewish experiences and connections in contemporary, inclusive presentations thoughtfully.
places.name_english: ANU – Museum of the Jewish People

opening_hours.notes: Times vary by season; check website. Group tours require advance reservation.

places.place_tip: Reserve timed tickets, start early, and pace galleries. Use audio guide, take breaks, and explore genealogy tools thoughtfully afterward.

places.name: Sarona Market & Templer Colony

Lawns and play areas welcome families while office towers rise around. Evenings buzz with tastings and music. A convenient stop for sampling cuisines, shopping local products, and relaxing between sights in central Tel Aviv.

opening_hours.notes: Vendor hours vary; weekends are busiest.

places.place_tip: Sample small portions from multiple stalls, carry water, and share dishes. Explore historic houses and lawns around the market gracefully.

places.name: Yarkon Park & River

Families picnic under trees while birds frequent wetlands. Bridges link lawns to amusement areas and climbing walls. A beloved green lung connecting neighborhoods to nature, exercise, and festivals across Tel Aviv’s northern reaches beautifully.

opening_hours.notes: Boat rentals, gardens, and attractions have separate hours and fees.

places.place_tip: Rent bikes or boats, bring sunscreen and water, and explore shaded paths. Check attraction hours and rentals ahead seasonally.

Hip eateries, bars, and vintage shops round out a lively neighborhood that celebrates experimentation, diversity, and community expression dynamically every week.

places.place_tip: Explore side alleys respectfully, avoid blocking doorways, and support local cafés. Consider a guided tour to decode artists’ signatures and themes.

Families enjoy open spaces, while evenings feature markets, music, and seasonal pop-ups near the waterfront.

places.place_tip: Arrive near sunset, browse shops, then walk to the beach. Check for markets, exhibitions, and live music on weekends.

attribution.title: Flag of Israel
attribution.author:
“The Provisional Council of State Proclamation of the Flag of the State of Israel” of 25 Tishrei 5709 (28 October 1948) provides the official specification for the design of the Israeli flag.
The color of the Magen David and the stripes of the Israeli flag is not precisely specified by the above legislation.  The color depicted in the current version of the image is typical of flags used in Israel today, although individual flags can and do vary.
The flag legislation officially specifies dimensions of 220 cm × 160 cm.  However, the sizes of actual flags vary (although the aspect ratio is usually retained).
attribution.description: Flag of Israel. Shows a Magen David (“Shield of David”) between two stripes. The Shield of David is a traditional Jewish symbol. The stripes symbolize a Jewish prayer shawl (tallit).

attribution.title: Coat of arms of the Ottoman Empire (1882–1922)
attribution.author: Juris Tiltins
attribution.credit: Own work  based on  Derivative works of this file:  Enver bey and Niyazi bey postcard 1908.jpg
attribution.description: Every sultan of the Ottoman Empire had his own monogram, called the tughra, which served as a royal symbol. A coat of arms in the European heraldic sense was created in the late 19th century. Hampton Court requested from the Ottoman Empire a coat of arms to be included in their collection. As the coat of arms had not been previously used in the Ottoman Empire, it was designed after this request, and the final design was adopted by Sultan Abdul Hamid II on 17 April 1882.
